strapline: A campaign song in the stands, a ruling in Solwezi and a vote in New York — all roads lead to Tuesday

stories.title: A song in the stands: the 'Pe Lampi' chants at Nkana bring a ministry warning, a FAZ threat — and a thermometer
stories.excerpt: A section of supporters at Nkana Stadium was reported to have sung the campaign song of the detained opposition figures during Saturday's 4–1 win. By Sunday the Sport Ministry had condemned it, FAZ had cited CAF and FIFA rulebooks, and the ruling party's Copperbelt chairman had called it 'hooliganism dressed in political colours'. Fred M'membe's answer: you cannot cure the fever by smashing the thermometer.

image.label: A song in the stands
image.caption: Nkana Stadium in Kitwe, where supporters were reported to have sung 'Pe Lampi' — the campaign song of the detained Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu — during Saturday's 4–1 win.

body: The chant has outlived the campaign, and now it has a government answer. On Saturday afternoon, during Nkana's 4–1 win over Makeni All Stars at Nkana Stadium in Kitwe, a section of supporters was reported to have sung "Pe Lampi" — the campaign song of Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu, the opposition figures in detention on sedition and treason charges. When the stadium floodlights briefly went off, phone lights went up. By Sunday evening the Ministry of Youth, Sport and Arts had formally condemned the chants, the Football Association of Zambia had cited CAF and FIFA rulebooks in warning of action, and the ruling party's Copperbelt chairman had called it hooliganism.

In a statement issued on Sunday 11 October, ministry permanent secretary Kangwa Chileshe said the conduct of some supporters during the match had been unacceptable and had no place in sport. The ministry warned that political activity at matches could provoke rival groups, create tension and possibly lead to violence, called on FAZ, the Zambia Premier League and clubs to caution their supporters, and said the Nkana scenes must not set a precedent. The statement named neither the song nor any individual.

body.text: Sport must not be used as a platform for advancing political agendas. Such conduct undermines the spirit of sport and risks turning football grounds into centres of political confrontation.
body.attribution: Kangwa Chileshe, permanent secretary at the Ministry of Youth, Sport and Arts, in Sunday's statement, quoted by Lusaka Times

body: FAZ general secretary Charles Chakatazya went further, grounding the association's position in Article 40(1) and 40(2) of the CAF Safety and Security Regulations — which prohibit the promotion of political messages inside or near a stadium, and ban political banners and symbols — Article 2(1)(l) of the CAF Statutes and Article 4(2) of the FIFA Statutes, which establish football's political neutrality. FAZ said it recognised the right to freedom of expression but stressed it must be exercised within football's regulations, and promised to work with authorities and stadium managers against individuals who breach stadium rules. It named no sanctions, no club and no start date.

body.text: Football belongs to all Zambians, regardless of their political affiliation. Our stadia must remain places where people come together to support their teams, not platforms for advancing political interests.
body.attribution: Charles Chakatazya, FAZ general secretary, quoted by Lusaka Times

body: The political divide answered in kind. Elisha Matambo, the UPND's Copperbelt provincial chairperson and a former Copperbelt minister, described the scenes as "hooliganism dressed in political colours", warning that the ruling party would not tolerate them at any venue in the province — "Not at Nkana. Not at Levy Mwanawasa Stadium" — and urging party members to report anyone chanting or displaying political symbols to police. He added that Zambia's national teams, including the women's side playing in Ndola on Tuesday, deserved "the full, united support of this nation, not a stage for political provocation". Fred M'membe, the Socialist Party leader, answered with a thermometer: "You can not cure the fever by smashing the thermometer." Before the election, he said, UPND supporters had chanted "Salt Sana" and "Bally" at matches, repeatedly and loudly, without interference; what was good for the goose, he said, must be good for the gander.

It is the second stadium in a fortnight where the song has been heard. Zambian Eye records that the first widely discussed episode came during Zambia's Africa Cup of Nations qualifier against Togo at Levy Mwanawasa Stadium in Ndola in late September, when a power disturbance darkened the floodlights — ZESCO said the interruption lasted a fraction of a second, though full brightness took about 20 minutes to return — and a section of the crowd chanted "Pe Lampi", some displaying the opposition campaign's symbol. M'membe said Zambians were using chants such as "Pelampi" and "Inyali" to express discontent, listing political repression, high fuel prices and the cost of living among what he called the real causes.

What follows is undecided. By Sunday evening, neither Nkana FC, the Zambia Premier League nor the police had publicly said what action, if any, would be taken; FAZ's statement promised enforcement without describing it. Zambian Eye's own analysis posed the harder question — who decides when a chant becomes political activity, and whether the same standard will apply to every slogan — while noting that no violence linked to the chants had been established. On the pitch, Nkana kept their perfect start to the transitional season: Emmanuel Silomba put Makeni ahead in the eighth minute, Michael Chapota equalised deep into first-half stoppage time, Lazarus Kambole scored twice and Nduna Zulu added the fourth in the 82nd minute.

body.title: The chant, the rules, the unanswered questions

FAZ cited Article 40 of the CAF Safety and Security Regulations and Article 4(2) of the FIFA Statutes in warning of enforcement. Similar chants were reported at the Zambia–Togo match in Ndola in late September. All per Lusaka Times, Zambia Monitor and Zambian Eye reporting.
body.unverified: The official statements named neither the song nor any individual; the chant's identity and its association with Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu come from the reporting, not from the ministry or FAZ. Who initiated the chants, and whether they were coordinated, is not established. Whether any supporter or club will actually be sanctioned is unknown.

stories.title: Election eve in New York: Zambia sells its rule-of-law record to the UN — and lobbies for a rights council seat
stories.excerpt: Justice permanent secretary Mwenya Kaela Bwalya told the UN General Assembly's Sixth Committee on Friday that the rule of law remains the bedrock of multilateral cooperation, listing new courts, judges and legal-aid expansion as proof. On the sidelines she lobbied for Zambia's Human Rights Council bid. The election is tomorrow.

image.label: Election eve
image.caption: The UN General Assembly's Sixth Committee heard Zambia's rule-of-law statement on Friday; the Human Rights Council election is Tuesday.

body: On the eve of the vote, Zambia made its case. Justice permanent secretary Mwenya Kaela Bwalya delivered the country's statement to the Sixth Committee of the 81st UN General Assembly on Friday, under agenda item 84 on the rule of law at national and international levels, telling delegates the rule of law remains the bedrock of multilateral cooperation, peace and sustainable development. She welcomed the secretary-general's report on strengthening and coordinating UN rule-of-law activities and the work of the International Law Commission, and said the international rule of law requires the greater inclusion of developing states in treaty-making.

The statement, issued through the Permanent Mission of Zambia to the United Nations, listed the reforms the Government wants the world to weigh: recent appointments of judges to superior courts, the construction of nine new courts, modifications to court infrastructure to improve accessibility, specialised bodies such as the Financial Crimes Court and the Economic and Financial Crimes Division, expanded Legal Aid Board offices and a computerised case-flow management system. Bwalya said the measures aim to turn equality before the law from an aspirational principle into a tangible right, to expedite justice for marginalised communities and to enhance judicial accountability — and that Zambia is aligning the reforms with the Grow Zambia agenda under the Eighth National Development Plan.

On the sidelines, Bwalya held bilateral meetings lobbying for Zambia's bid for a seat on the UN Human Rights Council for the 2027–2029 term, with elections scheduled for Tuesday 13 October at UN headquarters. The vote lands on the same day a Solwezi magistrate rules on jurisdiction in the sedition case against two detained opposition figures — a coincidence the Government's critics will not miss. As this newspaper reported on Saturday, UN special rapporteurs have raised concerns about the treason and sedition charges; the Government has answered that the matters are before the courts. Tuesday tests how the membership weighs the pitch against the headlines.

stories.title: The wait ends tomorrow: Solwezi rules on jurisdiction for Mundubile and Zulu — and the DPP has answered the critics
stories.excerpt: Principal Resident Magistrate Mambwe Mukonde will rule on Tuesday 13 October on whether her Solwezi court can hear the sedition case against Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu — and plea could follow. The State does not dispute that the alleged offence happened in Lusaka. Meanwhile, the DPP has a word for the delay critics: Shamwana took eleven months.

image.label: Tuesday at Solwezi
image.caption: Solwezi's magistrate's court, where the jurisdiction ruling in the Mundubile–Zulu sedition case lands on Tuesday 13 October.

body: One more night. Principal Resident Magistrate Mambwe Mukonde will on Tuesday 13 October rule on whether the Solwezi Magistrate's Court has jurisdiction to hear the sedition case against Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu — and, depending on the answer, plea could finally be taken. The ruling ends a procedural detour that began on 25 September, when the pair first appeared and the matter was adjourned because their lawyers were absent, and ran through last week's sessions, where the court declined to hear oral submissions, saying the issues had been adequately addressed in documents before it.

The defence argument is geography. Brian Mundubile, the losing 2026 presidential candidate, and his running mate Makebi Zulu face two counts of seditious practices contrary to Section 57, as read with Section 60, of the Penal Code — over Facebook livestreams in which Mundubile allegedly claimed victory on a parallel vote tabulation and called on the Electoral Commission of Zambia to resume counting, and in which Zulu allegedly said Mundubile would address the nation. They argue the alleged offences were committed in Lusaka, that trying them in North-Western Province breaches the Subordinate Courts Act and the Criminal Procedure Code, and that the venue blocks their witnesses and imposes financial hardship. On the location point, the State offered no resistance: Director of Public Prosecutions Gilbert Phiri told the court the prosecution did not dispute the warn-and-caution statements, which indicate the alleged offence was committed in Lusaka. The defence has also asked that constitutional questions be referred to the High Court — an application the State strongly opposes.

body.text: That's when the court will make its ruling on whether or not the court has got jurisdiction and whether or not this matter be referred to be heard in Lusaka.
body.attribution: Sakwiba Sikota, lead counsel for the defence, after the hearing, quoted by Lusaka Times

body.text: The DPP's answer to the delay critics

body: The wait itself has become an argument. The church and international bodies have called for a speedy trial for Mundubile, Zulu and 16 others — arrested in August and charged with treason in a separate matter headed for the High Court — all in detention since. Answering on Wednesday at a graduation ceremony for a financial investigations and asset recovery pilot course, DPP Gilbert Phiri attributed delays to investigations and called it a "cliché" to assume a suspect must appear in court days after arrest regardless of complexity. His precedent: the 1985 Shamwana treason case, which he said took eleven months to commence.

What Tuesday settles is venue, not guilt. If the magistrate finds for the defence, the sedition file moves towards Lusaka; if she finds for the State, plea could be taken in Solwezi the same day. Either way the treason case waits its own turn — and the State's position, stated in open court, that it does not dispute where the alleged offence happened will follow it to whichever courtroom hears it.

body.title: The road to Tuesday

6 October — oral submissions declined; written submissions ordered

The pair face two counts of seditious practices under Section 57 of the Penal Code; neither has taken plea. The State told the court it does not dispute that the warn-and-caution statements place the alleged offence in Lusaka. DPP Gilbert Phiri made his 'investigations take time' remarks on Wednesday 7 October, per News Diggers.

stories.title: Bracing for El Niño: Siame asks the World Bank to move from plans to investments — the Lobito Corridor on the table
stories.excerpt: Green Economy Minister Gilbert Siame received a senior World Bank delegation in Lusaka on Friday with two asks: support for the anticipated El Niño drought — forecasters say half the country is exposed — and accelerated green investment along the Lobito Corridor. The Bank says its response will be timely.

image.label: Bracing for El Niño
image.caption: Forecasters expect an El Niño drought across half of Zambia; the Government wants World Bank support before it lands.

body: The forecast is for half a country. Green Economy and Environment Minister Gilbert Siame received a senior World Bank Group delegation at his Lusaka office on Friday 9 October with a direct request: support for Zambia's response to the anticipated El Niño drought, including collaboration on early warning systems and vulnerability interventions. "This ministry, the World Meteorological Organisation and the SADC Climate Centre, we are all aligned that half of the country will have a drought," he said, per News Diggers. The delegation was led by Anna Wellenstein, the Bank's regional practice director for the Planet department in Eastern and Southern Africa, with Firas Raad, division director for Malawi, Tanzania, Zambia and Zimbabwe, country manager Martine Valcin and agriculture practice manager Frauke Jungbluth.

The second ask was the corridor. Siame urged the Bank to accelerate green investments along the Lobito Corridor — the rail-and-trade artery on which Zambia's target of three million metric tonnes of copper a year by 2030 partly rides — and welcomed support for the proposed Lobito Forest Economy Programme ahead of a mission scheduled for November 2026. His caution came with the request.

body.text: If infrastructure and mining expansion proceed without integrated land use planning and cumulative impact management, we risk undermining the very natural capital that sustains economic growth.
body.attribution: Gilbert Siame, Minister of Green Economy and Environment, quoted by Zambia Monitor

body: The partnership has numbers behind it. Siame cited the Eastern Province Jurisdictional Sustainable Landscape Programme, valued at about US$43 million and targeting nearly 29 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emission reductions by 2030, with 55 per cent of revenues directed to communities; and the US$137 million Transforming Landscapes for Resilience and Development Phase II — entirely grant-funded, implementing integrated landscape management across 32 districts and restoring degraded miombo ecosystems. "TRALARD II is not merely a project; it is a flagship reform platform," he said. He also called for continued cooperation on climate finance, carbon-market readiness under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, and capacity for the Zambia Environmental Management Agency and the Forestry Department.

The Bank's answer was warm but general. Raad said it was committed to projects that protect natural resources and create jobs, particularly for young people, and was working to ensure a timely response to the anticipated El Niño; Wellenstein called for a joint strategy to improve Zambia's access to climate finance; Valcin said the Bank was well placed to help attract foreign direct investment into the corridor. The memory doing the work in the room was 2024's: the drought that year was, per the Bank's own account, the worst in four decades, leaving more than 1.6 million households in need of emergency support and forcing a national disaster declaration — a fact no one in Friday's meeting needed to state.

stories.title: 'Monthly changes hurt planning': an energy expert backs the fuel-pricing review — and counts the VAT holiday's cost
stories.excerpt: Energy expert Johnston Chikwanda says the ERB's monthly price changes leave households and businesses unable to plan, and has welcomed the Government's promised review of the mechanism. But he backs the return of excise duty — the waivers were costing the Treasury — and notes VAT's suspension to December will cost a further US$120 million.

image.label: The pricing question
image.caption: Petrol is K31.46 a litre this month; the Government is reviewing the monthly mechanism that put it there.

body: The review now has an expert's seconding. Energy expert Johnston Chikwanda has welcomed the Government's plan to revisit the Energy Regulation Board's monthly fuel-pricing mechanism, telling ZNBC in an interview aired at the weekend that frequent price changes make it difficult for households and businesses to plan. He said Zambia should study how other countries manage reviews over longer periods — the same conclusion President Hichilema reached publicly on Friday, when he opened the 14th National Assembly and announced that the ERB's monthly pricing mechanism would be reviewed as part of establishing a secure, predictable and efficient petroleum-supply system.

On the tax question, Chikwanda sided with the Treasury. Restoring excise duty from October was necessary, he said, because the Government could not continue losing substantial revenue through waivers; the April-to-September suspension of excise duty and VAT on petrol and diesel had done its cushioning work but at a fiscal cost. Consumers still have one relief running: VAT on fuel remains suspended until December, a continuation Chikwanda said would see the Government forego a further US$120 million in revenue over that period.

The backdrop is the steepest single adjustment of the waiver era. The ERB's 30 September review restored excise duty and pushed petrol to K31.46 a litre (from K25.29) and diesel to K33.27 (from K26.86) — rises of almost a quarter in one step, driven by higher international prices, a kwacha that slipped from K19.28 to K19.76 to the dollar over the review period, and the tax's return. Bus fares followed upward on Friday, as this newspaper reported yesterday. The President's Friday address added two more pieces: government institutions will from now on acquire only electric vehicles — "Personally, I don't like it," he said of the monthly mechanism — with charging infrastructure to be built with the private sector, and the TAZAMA open-access pipeline system is to be strengthened.

What the review will actually change is not yet written. No date, terms of reference or preferred interval — two months, three months, or something else — has been announced; the details are expected through the Ministry of Energy and the 2027 Budget. What is dated is VAT: under the current statutory instruments it returns to fuel on 1 December, which would add a second tax line to the pump price unless the Treasury extends the relief again.

stories.title: 'Four, five hours without being attended to must not be heard of': Chilengi puts UTH on notice
stories.excerpt: Health Minister Roma Chilengi toured the University Teaching Hospital on Thursday and left with a warning: reports of patients waiting four to five hours for attention should not be heard of, accountability must be clear, and the management improvements already begun must be expedited.

image.label: Five hours too long
image.caption: University Teaching Hospital, Lusaka — where the Health Minister says four-to-five-hour waits 'should not be heard of'.

body: The minister came, saw — and set a standard. Health Minister Professor Roma Chilengi toured the University Teaching Hospital on Thursday 8 October and left with a public warning: reports of patients spending four to five hours without being attended to should not be heard of, and such cases would be taken with grief. The visit, to the country's biggest referral hospital, was covered by News Diggers and ZNBC.

body.text: There is need for clear accountability and I think we must improve management efforts that have already begun to put these things under control. They need to be expedited so that the investment that has gone in there can be put to use.
body.attribution: Professor Roma Chilengi, Minister of Health, during Thursday's UTH visit, quoted by News Diggers

body: ZNBC reported that the minister expressed concern at reports some patients spend more than five hours waiting to be attended to, and directed senior management to improve care and service. The message matches the ministry's current posture: the same minister fronts the health cooperation agreement signed with the United States last week — the pact under which 40,000 additional health workers are to be recruited — and its promises will be judged in waiting rooms like UTH's.

No deadline or sanction accompanied Thursday's directives. The minister framed the fix as acceleration, not overhaul: management efforts already begun should be expedited, he said, so that the investment that has gone into the hospital can be put to use. What patients will measure is simpler — the hours between arrival and attention.

stories.title: 'Selection on hunger, not names': Haalubono's promise on the eve of the Uganda decider
stories.excerpt: The Copper Queens host Uganda at Levy Mwanawasa Stadium on Tuesday at 18:00, trailing 2–1 from Kampala. Interim coach Charles Haalubono says selection will follow determination, not reputation — and captain Barbra Banda has told the senior players to fight for their places.

image.label: Ninety minutes
image.caption: Levy Mwanawasa Stadium, Ndola — Tuesday 13 October, 18:00: Zambia v Uganda, second leg.

body: Ninety minutes from either rescue or regret. The Copper Queens host Uganda's Crested Cranes at Levy Mwanawasa Stadium in Ndola on Tuesday 13 October at 18:00, trailing 2–1 from Thursday's first leg in Kampala and needing to overturn the deficit to reach the third round of the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic qualifiers. Ghana or Mauritius await the winner. The squad arrived back home at the weekend and trained at the match venue on Saturday evening, per FAZ, which has tickets on sale.

Interim coach Charles Haalubono's post-match reading in Kampala was blunt. Zambia, he said, lost control after taking the lead, improved in the second half after tactical changes to possession and movement, but failed to create clear scoring opportunities. He allowed one excuse — the artificial surface, for players more accustomed to natural grass — and took it away again by promising that selection for the return leg will be based on determination and willingness to fight for the national team rather than names or backgrounds. A Lusaka Times commentary made the same demand in starker terms: selection based on zeal, not reputation.

Captain Barbra Banda took the same line inward. The team would return to the drawing board to correct its mistakes, she said after the defeat; the result was not what Zambia wanted, but focus is on the return leg. She challenged the senior players to fight for their places after the young substitutes impressed in Kampala. For a side that has played at Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024, a third successive Olympics runs through Tuesday — and through a one-goal deficit against a team that fought, by the coach's own admission, harder than Zambia did.

stories.title: Operation Clear Path's ledger: 45 vendors fined, three City Market traders answer today
stories.excerpt: Lusaka City Council says 45 street vendors apprehended with police between 4 and 7 October have appeared before the Fast Track Court and been fined. Three more traders — who have stands in City Market but chose the street — appear before the same court today.

image.label: The clean-up ledger
image.caption: Lusaka's streets: 45 vendors fined by the Fast Track Court, three City Market traders answer on Monday.

body: The clean-up now has a court ledger. The Lusaka City Council says 45 street vendors apprehended between 4 and 7 October in a joint operation with the Zambia Police have appeared before the Fast Track Court and been fined for breaching street-vending regulations. Three other traders — people who hold stands in City Market but chose to sell from the street regardless — will appear before the same court today, Monday 12 October, council assistant public relations officer Nyambe Bulumba said in a statement issued on Saturday, per News Diggers.

The fines extend a pattern. A week ago, 25 vendors who resisted the anti-vending operation appeared before the Fast Track Court and were fined accordingly, the council said — the first court batch of an exercise that has also seen buses impounded in the central business district. Operation Clear Path, now the signature policy of Mayor Chitambala Mwewa's young tenure, aims to return pavements and roads to pedestrians and traffic; its critics' question — where the traders are supposed to go — remains formally unanswered, though the City Market three make the council's point for it: some of the street has a roof and chooses not to use it.

The council has framed the operation as a public-health measure as much as an order one, pointing to the city's cholera history whenever the vendors return to the pavements. The mismatch behind the cat-and-mouse is structural, and older than the operation: the Zambia Institute of Architects has estimated Lusaka's street-vending population in the hundreds of thousands against roughly eleven thousand designated market spaces. Until that arithmetic changes, the Fast Track Court is where the policy will keep its accounts.

stories.title: A night for the craft: MISA's media awards honour the newsroom — five prizes for ZNBC, a haul for the Daily Mail
stories.excerpt: The MISA Zambia Platinum and Golden Media Awards gala filled the Mika Convention Center on Friday night. ZNBC took five honours — Mark Ziligone the Golden Media Award for Television, Lucky Phiri overall best male journalist in school health reporting — and the Daily Mail's reporters shared in more than twenty awards given out.

image.label: A night for the craft
image.caption: The MISA Zambia Platinum and Golden Media Awards gala at Lusaka's Mika Convention Center on Friday 9 October.

body: The newsroom dressed up. The MISA Zambia Platinum and Golden Media Awards gala was held on Friday 9 October at the Mika Convention Center in Lusaka, the annual evening on which the Media Institute of Southern Africa's Zambian chapter honours reporting across print, radio and television. The gala's place on the calendar, around the International Day of Democracy, is deliberate — the craft's celebration tied to the freedoms that make it possible. By the weekend's count, the night's biggest institutional winners were the two state-owned newsrooms.

ZNBC reported five of its journalists honoured: Mark Ziligone won the Golden Media Award for Television, Lucky Phiri was named Overall Best Male Journalist in School Health Reporting, and Sibeso Likezo, Nyambe Nalishebo and Martha Kanene completed the broadcaster's roll. The Zambia Daily Mail's account, by reporter Zondiwe Mbewe, said several journalists had bagged more than twenty awards for outstanding contributions to journalism, with the state newspaper's own reporters receiving multiple honours.

The awards are MISA Zambia's annual honours for journalism across print, radio and television; the parent institute, founded in 1992, works on freedom of expression and access to information across Southern Africa. The school-health reporting categories — among ZNBC's wins — sat alongside the flagship Golden awards on Friday. The gala closes a week in which journalists of every house spent their days documenting the argument over what may be said, and sung, in public; Friday night, at least, belonged to the craft.

analysis.title: Where a chant ends and a rally begins
analysis.body: The ministry's worry is not invented: a month after a disputed election, with two opposition figures in detention, a stadium chant can be both symptom and spark, and CAF's neutrality rules — written for exactly this — exist to be cited. FAZ is right that the right to expression travels with the rulebook. The critics' case is also real: 'Salt Sana' rang through these same stadiums before the election with no ministry statement in reply, and M'membe's thermometer line lands because selective alarm is its own confession. What would settle the argument is not louder statements but a published, content-neutral stadium rule — what conduct is banned, what sanction follows, who decides — applied to 'Pe Lampi' and 'Bally' alike. Until then, every floodlight flicker will be read as politics, and every silence as favour. The clubs, told to control their supporters, will want the rule in writing before the next home game.

analysis.title: What Tuesday can and cannot settle
analysis.body: Two arguments converge tomorrow. In Solwezi, Magistrate Mukonde decides geography: whether a sedition case built on Facebook livestreams, which the State accepts were made in Lusaka, can be heard hundreds of kilometres to the north-west. A ruling for the defence moves the file to the capital; a ruling for the State could finally produce a plea, several court appearances after the first. What it cannot settle is the substance — the charges stand or fall at trial, not at the venue fight. Nor does it touch the heavier treason matter, which awaits the High Court on its own clock. The DPP's Shamwana precedent — eleven months to commence, in 1985 — is an answer about pace, not place. The critics' counter is custody: every month of process is a month of detention for the accused. Both things are true, which is why Tuesday's ruling, whatever it says, will be read as a verdict on more than jurisdiction.

analysis.title: The price of predictability
analysis.body: Monthly pricing was meant to keep the pump honest: track the oil price and the kwacha, pass both through, no hidden subsidy. Six months of tax relief bent that logic — the ERB's October board showed the market moving one way and policy another, and a 24-per-cent single-step rise is what 'smooth' looks like when the cushion expires. The case for a longer interval is planning: a bus operator or a farmer can price a quarter, not a midnight. The case against is exposure: if the kwacha slides for two months, a slower board either swallows the gap or springs a bigger jump. The Government's answer, so far, is a review without terms of reference, an excise duty restored and a VAT holiday with a December date — plus an electric-fleet promise that will not move this year's import bill. What the IMF's staff-level arithmetic assumes about the fuel line is the page everyone is waiting to read.
